ObjectName.value: California State Route 178 in Chicago Valley Outside of Death Valley National Park, California (15517288477)

Categories.value: California State Route 178|Aerial photographs of California|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation|Photographs by Ken Lund|Files uploaded by INeverCry

ImageDescription.value:
State Route 178 (SR 178) is a route that exists in two constructed segments. The gap in between segments is connected by various local roads and State Route 190 through Death Valley National Park.

SR 178 serves many different purposes. It connects SR 99 and Downtown Bakersfield with East Bakersfield and Lake Isabella. Lake Isabella is a weekend vacation spot for, among other things, fishing, boating, and white water rafting in the lake and Kern River. It is the only seasonal crossing and one of two crossings over the Sierra Nevada south of Yosemite (SR 120, Tioga Pass Road), connecting the southern San Joaquin Valley with the upper Mojave Desert and the Owens Valley. This also provides access to Death Valley National Park. If the unconstructed portion were built, it would also provide an easy route between Ridgecrest, California and Las Vegas, via Pahrump, Nevada.

This route is part of the California Freeway and Expressway System and is eligible for the State Scenic Highway System.

Built in 1904, it was designed by the San Francisco firm of Bliss & Faville, though little of their original design remains.

ImageDescription.value: This building was built in 1904 by the Kern County Land Company for the Hayden Furniture Company. originally designed to be 1 story, the plans were revised before construction began to add a second floor for use by the Ancient Order of United Workmen as a meeting hall. Designed by San Francisco architect Charles I. Havens, it is surprisingly intact, unlike many others destroyed in the 1952 earthquake.

ImageDescription.value: The Arthur S. Crites Building at the SW corner of 19th and Eye Streets. Originally built in 1901 by J.B. Berges for the Redlick Brothers department store who occupied the entire building until 1911. Designed by Orville Lee Clark, the building was originally a mixture of Italianate, Gothic and Beaux Arts (A historic photo of the building in the early 1900s (remove %7CA from URL to view)), featuring a corner tower. Arthur S. Crites purchased and remodeled the building into offices in 1937.
